items.title: Debounce
items.brief: Return a debounced version of fn: it runs only after wait ms have passed without another call, with the latest arguments and the caller's this.

tests.name: does not call fn immediately
tests.run: let n=0; const d=debounce(()=>n++, 30); d(); expect(n).toBe(0);

tests.name: calls fn once after a burst
tests.run: let n=0; const d=debounce(()=>n++, 30); d(); d(); d(); await wait(60); expect(n).toBe(1);

tests.name: uses the latest arguments
tests.run: let got; const d=debounce(x=>got=x, 30); d(1); d(2); d(3); await wait(60); expect(got).toBe(3);

tests.name: keeps this
tests.run: const o={v:7,got:null}; o.f=debounce(function(){ this.got=this.v; }, 20); o.f(); await wait(40); expect(o.got).toBe(7);

items.title: Throttle
items.brief: Return a throttled fn that runs at most once every wait ms. The first call runs right away; calls during the wait are ignored.

tests.name: first call runs immediately
tests.run: let n=0; const t=throttle(()=>n++, 40); t(); expect(n).toBe(1);

tests.name: calls inside the window are ignored
tests.run: let n=0; const t=throttle(()=>n++, 40); t(); t(); t(); expect(n).toBe(1);

tests.name: runs again after the window
tests.run: let n=0; const t=throttle(()=>n++, 30); t(); await wait(50); t(); expect(n).toBe(2);

items.title: Curry
items.brief: curry(fn) returns a function you can call with any grouping of arguments: f(1)(2)(3), f(1,2)(3) or f(1,2,3). It calls fn once it has fn.length arguments.

tests.name: partial calls are reusable
tests.run: const add=curry((a,b)=>a+b); const inc=add(1); expect(inc(1)).toBe(2); expect(inc(5)).toBe(6);

items.title: Memoize
items.brief: memoize(fn) caches results by the first argument so repeated calls with the same input don't recompute.

tests.name: computes once per input
tests.run: let n=0; const f=memoize(x=>{n++; return x+1;}); f(1); f(1); f(1); f(2); expect(n).toBe(2);

tests.name: caches falsy results too
tests.run: let n=0; const f=memoize(x=>{n++; return 0;}); f('a'); f('a'); expect(n).toBe(1);

items.title: Once
items.brief: once(fn) lets fn run only the first time. Later calls return the first result.

tests.name: runs only once
tests.run: let n=0; const f=once(()=>++n); f(); f(); f(); expect(n).toBe(1);

tests.name: returns the first result every time

items.title: Compose and pipe
items.brief: pipe(f, g, h)(x) returns h(g(f(x))): functions run left to right. (compose is the same, right to left.)

tests.name: works with strings
tests.run: const f=pipe(s=>s.trim(), s=>s.toUpperCase(), s=>s+'!'); expect(f('  hi ')).toBe('HI!');

items.title: Flatten an array
items.brief: flatten(arr, depth = 1) flattens nested arrays up to depth levels, like Array.prototype.flat. Use Infinity for fully flat.

items.title: Deep clone
items.brief: deepClone(value) copies plain objects and arrays at every level, so changing the copy never touches the original.

tests.name: nested objects are new
tests.run: const o={a:{b:1}}; const c=deepClone(o); c.a.b=2; expect(o.a.b).toBe(1);

tests.name: arrays are new
tests.run: const o=[[1],[2]]; const c=deepClone(o); c[0].push(9); expect(o[0]).toEqual([1]);

items.title: Deep equal
items.brief: deepEqual(a, b) returns true when two values have the same structure and primitive values (objects and arrays compared by content).

items.title: Promise.all
items.brief: promiseAll(items) resolves with all results in input order, or rejects as soon as one rejects. Items may be plain values.

tests.name: rejects on first failure
tests.run: let err; try{ await promiseAll([wait(50), Promise.reject('boom')]); }catch(e){ err=e; } expect(err).toBe('boom');

items.title: Promise.allSettled
items.brief: allSettled(items) waits for every item and resolves with {status:'fulfilled', value} or {status:'rejected', reason} for each, in order. It never rejects.

items.title: Promise.any / race
items.brief: promiseRace(items) settles the same way as the first item to settle, whether it resolves or rejects.

tests.name: first to reject wins
tests.run: let e; try{ await promiseRace([wait(40), new Promise((_,rej)=>setTimeout(()=>rej('no'),10))]); }catch(x){ e=x; } expect(e).toBe('no');

items.title: Retry a failing promise
items.brief: retry(fn, attempts) calls the async fn and, if it rejects, tries again until it succeeds or attempts run out (then rejects with the last error).

tests.name: succeeds after failures
tests.run: let n=0; const r=await retry(async()=>{ if(++n<3) throw 'fail'; return 'ok'; }, 5); expect(r).toBe('ok'); expect(n).toBe(3);

tests.name: gives up after attempts
tests.run: let n=0, e; try{ await retry(async()=>{ n++; throw 'nope'; }, 3); }catch(x){ e=x; } expect(n).toBe(3); expect(e).toBe('nope');

items.title: Sleep and timeout
items.brief: Write sleep(ms) that resolves after ms, and withTimeout(promise, ms) that rejects with 'timeout' if the promise takes longer.

tests.name: slow promise times out
tests.run: let e; try{ await withTimeout(sleep(80), 20); }catch(x){ e=x; } expect(e).toBe('timeout');

items.title: Map async with a concurrency limit
items.brief: mapLimit(items, limit, fn) runs the async fn over items with at most limit calls in flight, and resolves with results in input order.

tests.name: results in order
tests.run: const r=await mapLimit([30,10,20], 2, async x=>{ await wait(x); return x*2; }); expect(r).toEqual([60,20,40]);

tests.name: never exceeds the limit
tests.run: let live=0, peak=0; await mapLimit([1,2,3,4,5,6], 2, async x=>{ live++; peak=Math.max(peak,live); await wait(10); live--; }); expect(peak).toBe(2);

items.title: Event emitter
items.brief: Build an EventEmitter with on(name, fn), off(name, fn) and emit(name, ...args). on returns nothing; emit calls listeners in the order they were added.

tests.name: emit calls listeners with args
tests.run: const e=new EventEmitter(); let got; e.on('x',(a,b)=>got=a+b); e.emit('x',2,3); expect(got).toBe(5);

tests.name: multiple listeners in order
tests.run: const e=new EventEmitter(); const log=[]; e.on('x',()=>log.push(1)); e.on('x',()=>log.push(2)); e.emit('x'); expect(log).toEqual([1,2]);

tests.name: off removes a listener
tests.run: const e=new EventEmitter(); let n=0; const f=()=>n++; e.on('x',f); e.off('x',f); e.emit('x'); expect(n).toBe(0);

items.title: Function.prototype.bind
items.brief: Add Function.prototype.myBind(ctx, ...preset) that returns a function calling the original with this = ctx and the preset arguments first.

items.title: Function.prototype.call
items.brief: Implement Function.prototype.myCall(ctx, ...args) without using call, apply or bind. Hint: temporarily attach the function to ctx.

tests.name: sets this and passes args
tests.run: function f(a){ return this.v + a; } expect(f.myCall({v:1}, 2)).toBe(3);

items.title: Array.prototype.map
items.brief: Implement Array.prototype.myMap(callback, thisArg). The callback gets (value, index, array).

items.title: Array.prototype.reduce
items.brief: Implement Array.prototype.myReduce(callback, initial). Without an initial value, start from the first element; on an empty array with no initial, throw a TypeError.

items.title: Get a value by path
items.brief: get(obj, path, fallback) reads a nested value. path is 'a.b[0].c' or ['a','b','0','c']. Return fallback when any step is missing.

items.title: Chunk an array
items.brief: chunk(arr, size) splits an array into groups of size. The last group may be smaller.

items.title: Group by
items.brief: groupBy(items, keyFn) returns an object mapping each key to the items that produced it, in original order.

items.title: classNames
items.brief: classNames(...args) joins class names. Strings and numbers are kept, objects include keys with truthy values, arrays are flattened, falsy values are skipped.

items.title: LRU cache
items.brief: Build an LRUCache(capacity) with get(key) and put(key, value). When full, put removes the least recently used key. get returns -1 when missing.

tests.name: get and put
tests.run: const c=new LRUCache(2); c.put('a',1); expect(c.get('a')).toBe(1); expect(c.get('z')).toBe(-1);

tests.name: evicts least recently used
tests.run: const c=new LRUCache(2); c.put('a',1); c.put('b',2); c.get('a'); c.put('c',3); expect(c.get('b')).toBe(-1); expect(c.get('a')).toBe(1);

tests.name: updating a key refreshes it
tests.run: const c=new LRUCache(2); c.put('a',1); c.put('b',2); c.put('a',9); c.put('c',3); expect(c.get('a')).toBe(9); expect(c.get('b')).toBe(-1);

items.title: snake_case to camelCase
items.brief: toCamel(str) converts 'user_first_name' to 'userFirstName'. Then camelKeys(obj) converts every key of a (possibly nested) object.

items.title: Valid parentheses
items.brief: isValid(str) returns true when every (, [ and { is closed by the matching bracket in the right order.

items.title: Two sum
items.brief: twoSum(nums, target) returns the indices [i, j] of two numbers that add up to target, in one pass using a Map. Return null if there are none.

items.title: Binary search
items.brief: binarySearch(sorted, target) returns the index of target in a sorted array, or -1. It must be O(log n).

items.title: Reverse a linked list
items.brief: reverse(head) reverses a singly linked list of {value, next} nodes in place and returns the new head.

tests.name: reverses three nodes
tests.run: const l={value:1,next:{value:2,next:{value:3,next:null}}}; let r=reverse(l), out=[]; while(r){ out.push(r.value); r=r.next; } expect(out).toEqual([3,2,1]);

items.title: Private counter with a closure
items.brief: makeCounter(start = 0) returns {increment, decrement, value} where the count can't be changed from outside.

tests.name: counts up and down
tests.run: const c=makeCounter(); c.increment(); c.increment(); c.decrement(); expect(c.value()).toBe(1);

items.title: Remove duplicates
items.brief: unique(arr) returns the array without duplicate values, keeping the first occurrence order. Then uniqueBy(arr, keyFn) for objects.

items.title: Parse a query string
items.brief: parseQuery('?a=1&b=hello%20world&a=2') returns {a: ['1','2'], b: 'hello world'}. Repeated keys become arrays; values are decoded.

items.title: Your own new operator
items.brief: myNew(Ctor, ...args) does what new does: create an object linked to Ctor.prototype, run Ctor with it as this, and return it (unless Ctor returns its own object).

tests.name: links the prototype
tests.run: function P(){} P.prototype.hi=()=>'hi'; const p=myNew(P); expect(p.hi()).toBe('hi'); expect(p instanceof P).toBe(true);

items.title: Clean up an interval in useEffect
items.brief: A Clock component ticks every second. Fill in the effect so the interval starts on mount and is cleared on unmount.
items.explain: The empty dependency array runs the effect once after mount. Returning a cleanup function clears the interval on unmount, so it doesn't keep calling setNow on a removed component.

items.title: Functional state updates
items.brief: Clicking the button should add 3. Fill in the updater form so each update builds on the previous one.
items.explain: setCount(count + 1) three times uses the same stale count. The updater form receives the latest queued value each time. Pass the function itself to onClick, not addThree(), which would run during render.

items.title: usePrevious hook
items.brief: usePrevious(value) returns the value from the previous render.
items.explain: A ref keeps a value across renders without causing a re-render. The effect runs after render, so during the next render ref.current still holds the old value.

items.title: useDebounce hook
items.brief: useDebounce(value, delay) returns value only after it has stopped changing for delay ms.
items.explain: Every change of value schedules a timeout and the cleanup cancels the previous one, so only the last value within the delay window is stored.

items.title: Fetch without race conditions
items.brief: Show the user for userId. When userId changes quickly, ignore responses from older requests.
items.explain: Each effect run has its own ignore flag. When userId changes, the cleanup sets the old flag to true, so a slow old response can't overwrite the newer user.

items.title: Controlled input
items.brief: Make the input controlled by React state and show how many characters are typed.
items.explain: Start with an empty string (not null or undefined) so the input is controlled from the first render. value comes from state and onChange writes the new text back.

items.title: Stop needless re-renders
items.brief: Row only needs to re-render when its own item changes. Fill in the pieces that make memo actually work.
items.explain: React.memo skips re-rendering when props are shallow-equal. Without useCallback, handleSelect would be a new function every render and memo would never skip. A stable id makes a good key.

items.title: var in a loop with setTimeout
items.explain: var is function-scoped, so all three callbacks share one i. By the time they run, the loop has finished and i is 3. Using let creates a new binding per iteration and prints 0, 1, 2.

items.title: let in a loop with setTimeout
items.explain: let is block-scoped and each loop iteration gets its own copy of i, so each callback remembers a different value.

items.title: Sync, microtask, macrotask
items.explain: Synchronous code runs first (one, four). Then the microtask queue empties (the promise callback: three). Only then does the event loop take the next macrotask (the timeout: two).

items.title: async/await ordering
items.explain: An async function runs synchronously until its first await. The rest (B) is scheduled as a microtask, so C prints first.

items.title: Promise chain and setTimeout
items.explain: 5 is synchronous. Microtasks run in the order they were queued: the first then (2) and queueMicrotask (4). The second then (3) is only queued after 2 finishes. The timeout (1) runs last.

items.title: Hoisting a var
items.explain: The declaration var x is hoisted to the top of the scope and starts as undefined. The assignment stays where it is.

items.title: let and the temporal dead zone
items.explain: let and const are hoisted but stay uninitialized until their line runs (the temporal dead zone). Reading y before that throws a ReferenceError.

items.title: Function declaration vs expression
items.explain: Function declarations are hoisted with their body. For a function expression, only the var b is hoisted (as undefined).

items.title: this in methods vs arrow functions
items.explain: A regular method gets this from how it's called (obj). An arrow function has no this of its own; it uses the this of the code around the object literal, which is never obj. Copying the method doesn't change the function itself.

items.title: Losing this
items.explain: this is decided by the call site. Called as user.greet(), this is user. Called as a plain function in strict mode, this is undefined. call sets this explicitly.

items.title: typeof surprises
items.explain: typeof null is 'object' (a historic bug). Arrays are objects (use Array.isArray). NaN is a number value. Functions get their own 'function' result.

items.title: + and - with strings
items.explain: + with a string concatenates. -, * and other math operators convert both sides to numbers. true becomes 1.
Floating point can't represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance like Number.EPSILON, or round for display.

items.title: NaN comparisons
items.explain: NaN is never === to anything, itself included. Object.is and includes use SameValueZero-style checks that treat NaN as equal; indexOf uses === and can't find it.

items.title: Loose equality
items.explain: null == undefined is a special case (true), but null is not == 0. Strings and numbers are converted to numbers before comparing, so '' becomes 0 and '1' becomes 1.

items.title: Default sort
items.code:
console.log([10, 1, 5, 100].sort());
console.log([10, 1, 5, 100].sort((a, b) => a - b));
items.explain: Without a compare function, sort converts items to strings and sorts them alphabetically, so '100' comes before '5'. Pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.

items.title: ['1','2','3'].map(parseInt)
items.code: console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt));
items.explain: map passes (value, index). parseInt treats the index as the radix: parseInt('1', 0) is 1, parseInt('2', 1) is NaN (radix 1 is invalid), parseInt('3', 2) is NaN (3 isn't a binary digit).

items.title: References and copies
items.explain: b points to the same object as a. The spread copy c is shallow: it has its own n but shares the same inner object, so changing c.inner also changes a.inner.

items.title: foo.x = foo = {n: 2}
items.explain: The left side foo.x is resolved first, while foo still points to the original object. Then foo is reassigned to {n: 2}, and that new object is stored as x on the original object (still reachable as bar).

items.title: var a = b = 3
items.explain: This is var a = (b = 3). a is local to the function. b was never declared, so in sloppy mode it becomes a global variable that survives the function.

items.title: return on its own line
items.explain: Automatic semicolon insertion puts a semicolon right after a bare return, so foo2 returns undefined and the object below is dead code.

items.title: Closures keep their own state
items.explain: Each call to make() creates a new n. a has been called three times by the log, b once.

items.title: Array(3).map
items.explain: Array(3) creates three holes, and map skips holes. fill() turns them into real undefined values first. A leading comma in a literal also makes a hole.

items.title: Default parameters
items.explain: A default kicks in only when the argument is undefined (missing or passed explicitly as undefined). null is a real value and is kept.

items.title: const objects
items.explain: const stops reassigning the variable, not changing the object. Object.freeze stops changes; outside strict mode the write is silently ignored.

items.title: try / catch / finally return
items.explain: finally always runs before the function returns. If finally itself returns, that value replaces the one from try or catch.

items.title: split, reverse, join
items.code: console.log("i'm a lasagna hog".split('').reverse().join(''));
items.explain: split('') turns the string into characters, reverse flips the array and join('') glues it back together. The sentence is a palindrome-ish joke: reversed it reads 'go hang a salami'.

items.title: Generators
items.explain: The first next() runs to the first yield. The value passed to the second next() becomes the result of that yield, so x is 5. The third next() finishes the generator.

items.title: delete on an array
items.explain: delete removes the property but leaves a hole; length stays 3. filter skips holes. Use splice to really remove an item.
